brief.situation: TicketBurst sells concert tickets, now from separate AWS accounts under one organisation. A tour goes on sale at 10:00 today. Design before the doors open at 09:00: about 200 requests per second normally, 10x for the 40-minute rush, orders with RPO 1 minute and RTO 10 minutes even if the whole us-east-1 Region is impaired, card data never stored, the on-premises order-history database cut over to AWS this afternoon, and about $2,400 a month.
howItWorks: Place components into the edge, the public and private subnets of two Availability Zones, the regional services, a second Region (us-west-2) and the organisation (accounts and guardrails), and configure the Auto Scaling group.
You are not told which Availability Zone fails today. Design for either.

Then advance the clock event by event: doors open, a leaked deployment key, the on-sale spike, an AZ power loss, a Region impairment, a database host failure, the migration cutover, then finance asks for a 30% cut.
The debrief scores the SAP-C03 domains the day touched.

design.question: Before launch day: how does this design keep orders flowing through an AZ loss, a Region impairment and a leaked key, within RPO 1 minute and RTO 10 minutes, and how does the order history move off premises today?

parts.label: Multi-Region, governance and migration
parts.criteria: Names a warm standby (or active-active) in a second Region with health-checked DNS failover, a database replicated across Regions (Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB global tables) to meet RPO 1 minute, guardrails across accounts (Organizations SCPs) and backups copied to a locked vault in a separate account, and DMS with change data capture for a short cutover.
parts.modelAnswer: Inside us-east-1 every tier has a copy in two AZs, so either AZ can fail. For the Region, a warm standby in us-west-2 runs a small ASG behind its own ALB; Route 53 failover records with health checks move fans in about three minutes while it scales out. Orders live in an Aurora Global Database, whose secondary in us-west-2 trails by under a second, so a managed failover keeps RPO under a minute. Workloads and backups sit in separate accounts under AWS Organizations, with SCPs that deny deleting recovery points or stopping CloudTrail, and AWS Backup copies to a compliance-locked vault in the backup account. DMS runs a full load and change data capture from the on-premises database, so the afternoon cutover is a few minutes read-only.

expertPath.text: Route 53 with failover records and health checks, CloudFront and WAF; an ALB with a NAT gateway per AZ; an ASG in both AZs (min 4, max 16, m6i.large); an Aurora Global Database with its secondary in us-west-2; a warm standby in us-west-2; ElastiCache, SQS and S3; backups with PITR copied to a locked vault in the backup account; Organizations with SCP guardrails; DMS with CDC for the order history.
Scheduled scaling with a lower minimum, a Compute Savings Plan, reserved database and cache nodes, an S3 lifecycle rule and longer CloudFront TTLs; the second Region and the guardrails stay.

target.headline: TicketBurst sold out and stayed up, in either Region
target.body: Every requirement held through the leaked key, the spike, the AZ loss, the Region impairment, the database failure and the cutover, inside the budget.

harm.headline: A rough launch, and a useful one
harm.body: A failure broke RPO 1 minute or RTO 10 minutes, availability fell well below the SLA, or the bill ran more than 10% over. The event log shows which tier or Region was the single point.

scoring.modelReasoning: Inside us-east-1 every tier has a copy in two AZs, so the design survives whichever AZ fails. For the Region, a warm standby in us-west-2 with Route 53 health-checked failover takes traffic in about three minutes while it scales; an Aurora Global Database (or DynamoDB global tables) keeps the data within a second, so RPO 1 minute and RTO 10 minutes hold. Separate accounts under AWS Organizations with SCP guardrails stop a leaked deployment key from deleting backups or stopping CloudTrail, and a compliance-locked vault in the backup account keeps copies no one can delete. DMS with change data capture turns the order-history migration into a short read-only cutover. A pilot light is cheaper but needs tens of minutes; backup and restore needs hours and loses up to an hour of orders.
